newsitem.title: INDIA: India says sought army help to arrest politician.
newsitem.headline: India says sought army help to arrest politician.

text.p: India said on Friday its federal police had asked the army for help in arresting a powerful politician on embezzlement charges but the army refused to intervene.

"The army authorities...did not respond to the request on the ground that the army will be able to come to the aid of civil administration only at the request of the notified civil authorities," Home (Interior) Minister Indrajit Gupta said.

Gupta was speaking in parliament a day after lawmakers in the upper house said the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) had sought army assistance to arrest Laloo Prasad Yadav, former chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar.
Opposition lawmakers had called the CBI's move unconstitutional and dangerous, and demanded the government clarify the federal police's action.
The army is rarely called in to deal with political violence in India, although its troops often aid relief and rescue operations in natural disasters.

"The authority to call the army lies only with the governor of the state administration and, if it has happened, it is a serious matter and this should be enquired into," former prime minister Chandra Shekhar told parliament on Thursday.
"We are thankful to the army not only for refusing the request but also for protecting democracy," he said.

Other lawmakers said the CBI should have asked the Defence Ministry for permission. "There can be no involving the military authorities so long as the civil administration is in place," one opposition lawmaker said.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral had assured parliament that he would look into the matter.
Gupta said the CBI asked for army assistance only after Bihar's state police said it would take time to make necessary security arrangements.

Yadav, a charismatic low-caste leader, surrendered in a special CBI court on Wednesday after the agency issued a warrant for his arrest in a $280 million embezzlement scandal. Yadav says he is innocent.
Hundreds of his supporters lay prostrate or squatted in the street outside the court to try to block a police convoy carrying Yadav to jail. Many beat their heads on the hoods of police vehicles.
Some 5,000 paramilitary troops fanned out across Bihar on Friday as Yadav's supporters barricaded roads and clashed with baton-wielding policemen in protests against his arrest.
Electoral violence and political corruption are rampant in populous, economically backward Bihar. Bad roads make many of its villages inaccessible to any central legal authority.
